extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and advanced graduate students (number theory, geometry, analysis, algebra)
extracted.subtask_description: A list and discussion of foundational research problems and axiomatic/questions across many branches of mathematics (geometry, group theory, analysis, number theory, algebra, topology) intended to set directions for future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minkowski geometry — equal-distance locus
rubrics_metrics.description: Points at equal distances from a fixed point O lie on a convex closed surface of ordinary Euclidean space with O as a center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stipulation characterizes one aspect of Minkowski's geometry as an alternative to ordinary Euclidean geometry; it is offered as an axiom-like requirement for defining distance in that geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minkowski geometry — equality of segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Two segments are said to be equal when one can be carried into the other by a translation of the ordinary Euclidean space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines segment equality in Minkowski's geometry via translations rather than Euclidean congruence motions; used as a basic stipulation in the geometry's foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of the parallel axiom in Minkowski geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: In Minkowski’s geometry the axiom of parallels also holds (as in Euclidean geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts this with geometries obtained by studying the straight line as shortest connection, which can violate the parallel axiom while still satisfying other Minkowski axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity conditions for 'straight line is shortest path' theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate the precise conditions under which the theorem that the straight line is the shortest path between two points (and Euclid's equivalent about triangle sides) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasizes that studying these conditions will illuminate the idea of distance and the plane, and can lead to construction of systematic geometries; investigating compatibility and limits of this theorem is desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lie's finite continuous group — closure/composition property
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite continuous group of transformations is a system x'i = fi(x, a1,..,ar) such that the successive application of any two transformations of the system yields another transformation of the same system, expressible as x''i = fi(x; c1(..),..,cr(..)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The group property is expressed by functional equations relating the parameter-composition functions c1,..,cr; this is Lie's defining structural requirement for a continuous transformation group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lie's differentiability assumption and its role
rubrics_metrics.description: Lie assumes differentiability of the functions defining the group; derivation of fundamental differential equations uses continuity and differentiability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert raises the question whether differentiability is essential to Lie’s theory, or whether it can be derived from the group concept plus other geometric axioms; he suggests retaining continuity but questioning differentiability as a primitive assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to analytic (differentiable) groups under transitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to analytic groups is possible when the group is transitive and the existence of the first and certain second derivatives of the defining functions is assumed (Lie announced; Schur proved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a theorem about when a given continuous group can be transformed into one with differentiable defining functions; Hilbert cites Lie's announcement and Schur's proof for finite transitive groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate differentiability assumptions for infinite groups
rubrics_metrics.description: For infinite transformation groups, explore whether analogous reduction to differentiable/analytic groups is possible without assuming differentiability a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads into the broader study of functional equations (Abel, difference equations) typically treated under differentiability assumptions — Hilbert urges examination without such assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional equations and differentiability (Minkowski/Cauchy example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minkowski starts with the functional equation f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y) and succeeds in proving existence of certain differential quotients for f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates that some functional equations imply differentiability-like consequences; but Hilbert also notes existence of analytic functional equations whose only solutions are non-differentiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of non-differentiable solutions to analytic functional equations
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist analytic functional equations whose sole solutions are non-differentiable functions (examples via trigonometric series, Borel/Picard constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert emphasizes that not all functional equations that look analytic force differentiability; this motivates study of functional equations without differentiability assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatization of physical sciences (probability & mechanics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat physical sciences (notably probability theory and mechanics) in the same axiomatic manner as geometry: find small sets of axioms that cover wide classes of phenomena and then adjoin axioms for more special theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert calls for logical investigation of probability axioms, rigorous development of method of mean values (kinetic theory of gases), and mathematical foundations of mechanics including limiting processes from atomistic to continuum theories; also stresses testing compatibility of new axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility testing of newly introduced axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematician's duty: to test exactly in each instance whether new axioms are compatible with previous ones, not relying solely on physical intuition or experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert argues that proving compatibility forces precise formulation of axioms and is important for rigorous theory-building in physical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 7: Irrationality and transcendence of certain numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate further Hermite and Lindemann-type results: determine transcendence/irrationality of special numbers and transcendental functions taking algebraic values at algebraic points (e.g., whether e^{α} with algebraic α and irrational algebraic exponent is transcendental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert points to examples (geometry-formulated statement about isosceles triangles) and expects new methods will be required to prove such statements about special irrational and transcendental numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 8: Problems of prime numbers (Riemann hypothesis and consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove Riemann's assertion that the nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) have real part 1/2; refine Riemann's prime-counting formula, study the error term (order ≤ 1/2 in x), and investigate whether observed condensations of primes relate to terms from low complex zeros; pursue Goldbach, twin primes, and representation of affine linear diophantine equations in primes; apply prime-distribution results to ideal primes in number fields (ζ_k(s)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert lists both specific conjectures (Riemann hypothesis) and related goals (Goldbach, twin primes, distribution in number fields) and suggests deeper understanding of Riemann’s series and its terms is central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 9: Proof of the most general law of reciprocity in any number field
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove reciprocity laws for residues of l-th powers in any number field: for l an odd prime, for powers of 2, and for powers of odd primes; generalize tools (theory of l-th roots of unity, relative quadratic fields) to achieve this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert expects the law and its proofs to arise by suitable generalization of existing number-field theories developed by himself and others; he regards this as central to algebraic number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 10: Algorithmic determination of solvability of Diophantine equations
rubrics_metrics.description: Devise a process by which, in a finite number of operations, one can determine whether a given Diophantine equation with integer coefficients is solvable in integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert asks for a decision procedure (finite algorithm) for integer solvability of arbitrary Diophantine equations — a problem about decidability in number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 11: Quadratic forms with algebraic numerical coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop theory of quadratic forms with any number of variables and with any algebraic numerical coefficients: in particular solve such quadratic equations in integers or fractions belonging to the algebraic field determined by the coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes that progress in quadratic number fields enables attacking general quadratic forms; goal includes expressing solutions within the corresponding algebraic realm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 12: Extend Kronecker’s theorem on abelian fields to arbitrary algebraic fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalize Kronecker's result (abelian number fields arise from composition of fields of roots of unity; exponential function gives numbers for rational field; elliptic modular functions for imaginary quadratic fields) to arbitrary algebraic fields of rationality, connecting arithmetic (class field theory) and function-theoretic parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert highlights two parts (arithmetical determination of equations by group/discriminant and function-theoretical generation) and suggests using reciprocity laws and analogies between algebraic functions and algebraic numbers; he points to complex multiplication and other prior works as keys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 13: Impossibility of solving general 7th-degree equation with functions of two arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the general equation of the seventh degree cannot be solved by functions depending only on two arguments (i.e., is not representable by a finite chain of functions of two variables as in nomography); contrast with solvability of general 5th and 6th degree via Tschirnhausen transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert explains nomography and how many functions can be constructed by finite insertions of two-argument functions; he believes the 7th-degree root is not of this class and notes work constructing analytic functions of three arguments not obtainable from two-argument chains; nomographic methods with movable elements can extend constructions (d’Ocagne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 14: Finiteness of complete systems of relatively integral functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given rational integral functions X1,..,Xm of variables x1..xn (substitution S), decide whether all rational functions of X1..Xm that become integral after substitution (i.e., relatively integral functions) always form a finite field of integrality (i.e., can be generated by finitely many such functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert frames a refined arithmetic version (coefficients integral, prime-power conditions) and gives particular cases showing finiteness for fixed exponents but asks about uniform finiteness across exponents; this connects to finiteness theorems in invariant theory and elimination theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 15: Rigorous foundation of Schubert's enumerative calculus
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish rigorously (with exact limits of validity) the enumerative numbers Schubert computed using the principle of special position/conservation of number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although elimination algebra in principle suffices, Hilbert emphasizes needing carried-out elimination for special-form equations so that degrees of final equations and multiplicities of solutions are predictable; greater rigor is required for enumerative geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 16: Topology of algebraic curves and surfaces and limit cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the maximum number and mutual positions of components (closed separate branches) of plane algebraic curves of order n (beyond Harnack’s bound), relative positions for maximal cases (examples for 6th-order), and analogous questions for sheets of algebraic surfaces; also determine maximum number and positions of Poincaré limit cycles for first-order differential equations dy/dx = Y/X where X,Y are rational integral functions of degree n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert notes partial results (Harnack, his own work for 6th order) and calls for thorough investigation of relative positions and counterparts in 3D surfaces; he explicitly connects these algebraic-topological questions to topology of families of curves from differential equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 17: Expression of definite forms by squares (sums/quotients of squares)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize when a rational integral definite form (never negative) can be expressed as a sum of squares of forms or as a quotient of sums of squares of forms; ask whether the coefficients in such representations can be taken from the same field of rationality as the form's coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert recalls his results showing not every definite form is a sum of squares but notes positive results for ternary forms and calls for understanding representations as quotients of sums of squares and arithmetic restrictions on coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem 18: Building space from congruent polyhedra (classification of motion groups with fundamental regions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate groups of motions in plane and space for which a fundamental region exists, classify essentially different kinds of fundamental regions and determine whether in n-dimensional Euclidean space there are only finitely many essentially different kinds of motion groups with a fundamental region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert compares elliptic, Euclidean, and hyperbolic cases: elliptic has finitely many kinds and finite number of congruent regions suffice; hyperbolic has infinitely many; Euclidean sits between. For 3D and n-dimensional Euclidean space he references results and poses the finiteness-question for general n, noting difficulties in generalizing Euclidean case.
